summary: The note describes the U.S. response to Japan's expansion before the attack on Pearl Harbor. Beginning in 1938 the U.S. imposed increasingly restrictive trade measures on Japan, including ending its 1911 commercial treaty in 1939 and tightening export controls with the Export Control Act of 1940. These measures did not stop Japan's war in China or its signing of the Tripartite Pact with Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy in 1940, which formed the Axis Powers.
one_line: Overview of escalating U.S. trade restrictions on Japan from 1938 and Japan's 1940 alignment with the Axis via the Tripartite Pact.
key_facts: Beginning in 1938, the U.S. adopted a succession of increasingly restrictive trade restrictions with Japan.
The U.S. terminated its 1911 commercial treaty with Japan in 1939.
The 1939 termination of the U.S.-Japan commercial treaty was further tightened by the Export Control Act of 1940.
The U.S. trade restrictions failed to deter Japan from continuing its war in China.
The U.S. trade restrictions failed to deter Japan from signing the Tripartite Pact in 1940.
Japan signed the Tripartite Pact in 1940 with Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy.
The Tripartite Pact officially formed the Axis Powers.
The Tripartite Pact was signed in 1940.
